From twelve to eighteen or nineteen: only a few years.

For an adult looking back, it fits into a single line of a résumé. For a teenager, it is almost an entire age. Height changes, voice changes, even the way you look at people changes. Adults once seen only by looking up suddenly seem less imposing; the university entrance exam that once felt impossibly distant comes closer day by day.
Zhang Yuansheng went through that transformation in the residential communities of Shengli Oilfield.

Little by little, people stopped thinking of him as “the kid who just moved here from Xiazhang.” Classmates, teachers, the route to and from school, the rhythm of family life, and the distinctive tempo of the oilfield slowly stitched a new identity onto him.
The strangest thing about adolescence is that while people feel they are already grown, they keep doing things that, looking back, make no sense at all.
Like walking out on winter ice.

Winters in the oilfield were hard and windy. When shallow water froze, children quickly turned it into a playground. First they tested it with a heel, then stamped twice. If the ice did not crack, courage rose another level. Once one child walked farther out, the others did not want to look afraid.

One winter, several boys stood at the edge of a frozen stretch of water. The ice was dark below; no one could tell how deep it was. Near the bank it was solid, and someone had already slid out and back safely.
Yuansheng stepped onto it too.
At first, the ice made only a faint cracking sound.
“It’s fine,” someone ahead said.
No one wanted to be the first to turn back.
A few more steps, and the sound changed.
Not a crackle.
A short, dull break.
When Yuansheng looked down, a black line was racing outward from in front of his shoe.
He had no time even to step back.
The surface vanished beneath him.
Icy water surged to his waist.

The cold did not arrive slowly. In that instant it was like an enormous iron plate striking his chest, knocking the breath out of him and almost taking command away from his legs. His hands grabbed the rim of the ice by instinct, but whenever he put weight on it, the edge broke.
He tried to climb. The ice split.
He tried again. It split again.
The boys on shore began shouting.
This time no one laughed.
Someone lay flat and edged forward. Someone else threw him a wooden pole found from somewhere nearby. Yuansheng missed it the first time; it slid past his hand.
The water quickly soaked through his padded trousers. As the clothes absorbed water they grew heavy, and he could feel his body being pulled downward.
The pole came toward him a second time.
He caught it with both hands.
“Don’t let go!”
The boys on shore pulled backward. The one nearest the hole did not dare stand, and could only inch away on his stomach. The ice cracked all along beneath them with a sound that made the teeth ache.
At last, Yuansheng’s upper body slid back onto the ice.
First his chest, then his waist, and finally two waterlogged legs came out of the black opening.
He lay there gasping, cheek against the ice, and somehow the ice felt warmer than the water.

The walk home became a different kind of ordeal. The wind hit his soaked trouser legs and they quickly stiffened. Every step squeezed water inside his shoes. The boys discussed the same question all the way back: how were they going to explain this?
In summer, falling into water could be explained as stepping into a ditch.
In winter, when your entire body was soaked, lying became more difficult.

When he got home, the adults’ reaction was of course nothing like the literary memory he would later make of it. There was no embrace, no “thank heaven.” Most likely they first demanded to know where he had been, then scolded him, then hurried to change his clothes and warm him by the fire.
That is often how ordinary families respond to a brush with death: warm the person first, settle the account afterward.
That night, lying under the quilt, his legs still felt faintly cold.
The water of Zhaojiadian, the tyre on the oilfield road, and the broken winter ice were three entirely different forms of danger.
They did not turn him into someone who believed he had unusually good luck. A child does not summarize life that way.
They simply left behind a primitive lesson: before many things truly go wrong, they look perfectly fine.

Later, as a warehouse manager, he would become unusually sensitive to “almost.” A shipment placed almost correctly, a number almost matching, one wrong character in a roll number—today it might seem small; tomorrow someone could spend half a day searching for something that had vanished into the system. That habit decades later was not taught by one sheet of ice, of course, but caution is often worn into a person by countless moments of “almost.”
Outside danger, most days were still ordinary.
His parents’ generation did not have complicated expectations for children: study, get admitted somewhere, and find a stable future.

In those years, the phrase “test your way out” carried a weight difficult to reproduce later. Ordinary families had few resources with which to lay out a road for their children. Exams therefore felt brutally direct. A single paper, a difference of a few dozen points, could send young people toward entirely different lives.

Zhang Yuansheng was not a boy who had spent every day bent over books, deaf to everything outside the window. Real youth is never that neat. He played too much sometimes, lost focus, liked some classes, and merely endured others. When boys gathered together, who was brave, who could run fastest, and who had just embarrassed himself mattered far more than what career any of them might have ten years later.
But he had one quality that never quite left him: once he decided something ought to be done, he was willing to keep working at it little by little.

Back then it was not called “self-discipline.” There were no timers, spreadsheets, or planning apps. A problem not understood today could be looked at again tomorrow. Something done badly once could be tried again. Whether anyone noticed was usually not the most important thing.
His father rarely sat him down for long speeches either.

Much of the education in that household did not come through heart-to-heart talks. It came through life itself: his father went to work every day; his mother kept the household running. If something was there to be done, someone had to do it.
As eighteen approached, the air of life tightened.

The university entrance exam was no longer merely a word teachers repeated. It was a door coming closer every day. Classmates still joked on the surface, but each was quietly calculating. Some wanted big cities. Some only wanted any university at all. Some said they did not care, then went home more anxious than anyone.
Yuansheng began to imagine university too.

His picture was vague: a few classroom buildings, a dormitory shared by several people, a library much larger than the one at school. What truly attracted him was the idea of a life in which, for the first time, he could decide a little more for himself.
Leaving Zhaojiadian at twelve had been a decision made by adults.
This time, he wanted his own exam score to carry him out.
1990 arrived.

The classroom in June was hot. Even with the electric fans turning, they only stirred the heat from one side of the room to the other. Draft paper stuck to wrists. Palms sweated. Pens became slippery after being held too long.
The world outside was changing quickly, but for a young person preparing for an exam, even the largest era eventually shrank onto a sheet of paper.
When the final exam ended, no music began to play.

Some students rushed out and immediately compared answers. Others refused to discuss a single question. Zhang Yuansheng stepped through the door and, with years of pressure suddenly left without an object, felt empty for a moment.
Then came waiting again.
Waiting for scores, waiting for admission, waiting for a letter that would truly determine where the next stop would be.
He did not know that childhood had already nearly kept him from reaching this day three times.
To him then, the most life-or-death question was whether the admission letter would arrive.
That is how youth works.
The deaths you have already escaped are quickly forgotten. The future you have not yet received can keep you awake all night.
